title: Atomic-Scale Structural Insights to Optical Anisotropy in Quasi-One-Dimensional Hexagonal Chalcogenides via Electron Ptychography
content: Optical anisotropy is a fundamental property employed in linear and non-linear optics, characterized by direction-dependent differences in the real part and imaginary component of complex refractive indices (n + iκ), which manifest as birefringence (Δn) and dichroism (Δκ), respectively [1]. Quasi-one-dimensional (quasi-1-D) birefringent chalcogenide materials, such as BaTiX3 (X=S, Se), feature parallel chain-like structures composed of face-shared TiS6 octahedra running along the c-axis, and exhibit pronounced optical anisotropy between the inter-chain (a-b plane) and intra-chain (c-axis) orientations (Figure 1A) [2]. Their record-high birefringence makes them promising candidates for non-linear photonic devices. Recent studies suggest that their distinctive optical properties and multiple phase transitions are closely linked to atomic displacements within the TiS₆ octahedra [2-4].
